fields.expected:
Most of what I've built lately comes back to retrieval and judgment. In tSearch, I built a talent-discovery pipeline that starts from seed candidates, expands through public GitHub and Substack collaboration graphs, scores heuristically, and only then runs rubric-driven LLM judges. The hardest part was not generation, it was retrieval quality and deciding what counts as evidence. I made "insufficient evidence" a real output rather than a low score, because a search system that quietly guesses is worse than one that says it doesn't know. I hit the same wall at Intelehealth, where I built an evaluation framework over a 4,169-case clinical benchmark and found that producing an answer was cheap while deciding whether to trust it was the actual problem.

That's why Exa interests me. If AI makes generation abundant, the bottleneck moves to finding and verifying the right information, and Exa is building the layer underneath that: crawling the whole web, training embedding models, and making retrieval fast enough to actually use. I'd want to work on the retrieval and evaluation side, and I like that the work has real users, real failure modes, and things I can measure.

fields.expected: ClarityAtlas, the iOS health app I built as technical lead at Open Health Intelligence. The technical part I'm most proud of is passive sleep estimation without a wearable. Most sleep tracking assumes a watch, so I built an estimator from phone-interaction and motion signals using HealthKit and Core Motion inputs like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns. I also built the backend for behavioral comparison, including a "Sleep Twins" matcher that standardizes behavioral features and matches users by weighted distance, so someone sees their sleep in context instead of as an isolated number. I wrote the whole thing in Swift and SwiftUI on Supabase and shipped it into a live pilot at Hopkins with 30 or more users. What I actually learned is that the build was maybe half the work. Getting real users, refining the thesis, and explaining repeatedly why the thing should exist mattered just as much. We got our meeting with President Daniels by spotting him during Lighting of the Quads and knocking on the doors of Garland Hall until someone let us pitch.

fields.expected:
Mostly two things. The first is building something that actually gets used, not demoed. With SnapSort I learned that a technically functional system and a product people use are very different; I got it to 300+ users and most of the work was pricing, positioning, and fixing the parts that broke for real people. The same lesson showed up at Open Health Intelligence, where getting 30+ users into a pilot took as much stakeholder work as engineering.

The second is the question I keep circling back to: as AI makes generation cheap, judgment becomes the scarce thing. That came out of Intelehealth, where I built an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard using stratified sampling. Producing an answer was fast; deciding whether to trust it was the hard problem. It shows up again in my job-application agent, where free-text and demographic fields are architecturally blocked from autofill and always escalate to a human.

I'm motivated by problems with a concrete user, a real failure mode, and a system I can test against reality rather than against a fixture.
